title: Behind the Lens: a wildlife photographer

script.text: This week on Behind the Lens my guest is Anna Kowalski, a wildlife photographer whose pictures have appeared in magazines all over Europe. Anna, welcome.
You started when you were fourteen. What did you photograph first?

Our neighbour's cat, if you can believe it. My grandfather gave me an old camera, and for months I photographed anything that moved in the garden: sparrows, hedgehogs, a very unfriendly squirrel. Most of the pictures were awful, but one of the hedgehogs won a school competition, and that was the moment I thought it might be more than a hobby.
Wildlife photography sounds romantic. What is the reality?

Mostly waiting. I once spent nine days in a tiny shelter in the Carpathians hoping to photograph a lynx, and I never saw one. I came home with pictures of fog. People imagine adventure, but the work is largely patience, cold feet and cold sandwiches.

Less than you'd think. The worst moment was in Norway, when I misjudged the ice on a frozen lake and fell through up to my waist. Fortunately my guide was close. Since then I always travel with a partner, whatever the location.
Many photographers now use drones. What do you think of that?

I have mixed feelings. Drones allow pictures that were impossible before, such as a bird's-eye view of a migrating herd. But they can frighten animals, especially birds with nests, so I only use one where it's permitted and never near breeding colonies. A good picture is never worth disturbing a living creature.
What about editing? Is it acceptable to improve a photograph with software?

Small corrections, yes: brightness, cropping, removing dust. What's unacceptable is adding things that weren't there. A few years ago a famous competition withdrew an award because the winner had moved an animal into the picture. It destroyed his reputation overnight, and rightly so.
What equipment would you recommend for a beginner?

Honestly, nothing expensive. A modern phone has an excellent camera, and what matters in the beginning is learning to look: how light falls, how an animal moves, when to press the button. I know professionals who still do their best work with one cheap lens.
And finally, what are you working on now?
A project about urban wildlife: foxes in car parks, falcons on skyscrapers. It's important to show that nature isn't something far away; it's all around us, if we pay attention.
Anna Kowalski, thank you very much.

questions.q: What does Anna say about her trip to the Carpathians?
options: She eventually succeeded in capturing an image of a lynx.
She came back without the pictures she wanted.
She had to leave early because of illness.

options: She now always works with a companion.
A guide had warned her about the ice.
She now avoids travelling to cold regions.

options: They should be banned from nature reserves.
They are acceptable if used with care.

options: Concentrate on learning to observe.
Buy a professional camera as soon as possible.
Photograph pets before wild animals.

discuss: Anna says that waiting is the main part of her job. Are you a patient person?
Would you like to be a photographer or an explorer? Why?
Is it acceptable to edit photographs? Where is the line?
